drills.q: Name the three distinct reproducibility gaps that experiment tracking, model registry, and data versioning each close.
drills.a: Tracking = reproduce a run (code/params/metrics). Model registry = govern which artifact is live where. Data versioning = reproduce the exact input data used.

drills.q: True or false: MLflow model registry stages let a single version hold both 'staging' and a canary role simultaneously.
drills.a: False -- stages are exclusive, one per version. That limitation is exactly why MLflow deprecated stages in favor of multi-assignable aliases.

drills.q: Which company acquired the DVC open-source project, and when?
drills.a: lakeFS acquired DVC from Iterative.ai on November 18, 2025.

drills.q: A 10-person team is deciding between W&B Teams and self-hosted MLflow. What's the rough monthly cost comparison, and what does the MLflow number leave out?
drills.a: W&B Teams ~$500/mo for 10 seats (~$50/user/mo). Self-hosted MLflow: ~$150-500/mo infra, but that excludes engineer time for setup/maintenance/on-call, which often exceeds the infra cost itself.

drills.q: Explain mechanically why DVC's checkout model doesn't scale well to a multi-TB data lake, and what LakeFS does differently.
drills.a: DVC checkout materializes real local file copies resolved from .dvc pointers -- copy-on-checkout, fine at GB scale, slow/expensive at TB+ scale. LakeFS implements branch/commit/merge as metadata operations directly over the object store with zero-copy branching, so creating an isolated branch is instant with no storage duplication.

drills.q: Why is a prompt change treated as having the same 'blast radius' as a model weight change?
drills.a: A wording change (added example, reordered instructions) can shift output quality, safety behavior, and token cost as significantly as swapping model weights -- but a prompt is far easier to edit with zero review gate since it's often just an inline string with no version history.

drills.q: A model's registry entry shows the artifact but no data-version tag on its originating run. Six months later, someone needs to explain why the model behaves a certain way. What's broken?
drills.a: The lineage chain is broken at the data-version link -- you have the weights but no reproducible path back to the exact training data snapshot, which blocks retraining, auditing, or explaining behavior tied to specific data characteristics.

drills.q: Design the promotion flow for a new model version using aliases instead of stages, including an eval gate. What's the atomic operation that makes rollback cheap?
drills.a: Register the version from a run's artifact, tag it 'candidate', run eval and check against a threshold, then reassign the 'champion' alias to it if it passes. Serving code resolves models:/name@champion at load time. Rollback = reassigning 'champion' back to the prior version, a single atomic registry operation, no redeploy.

drills.q: A prompt registry shows 'production' pointing at v14, but deployed behavior doesn't match v14's content. Walk through the debugging order.
drills.a: First check whether serving code actually resolves the alias at request/load time vs. caching or hardcoding an older version at deploy time. Second, check for a second code path pointed at a different alias or pinned version. Third, confirm the alias reassignment itself succeeded and targeted the right registered prompt name. If all check out, suspect the underlying model (a pinned model alias moved, or non-determinism at temperature>0) rather than the prompt registry.

drills.q: A team wants to skip a prompt registry because they deploy often and it 'feels like overhead.' Make the counter-argument, and state what would legitimately change your mind.
drills.a: Frequent deploys are exactly when prompt regressions are hardest to catch -- no diff between the working prompt and what shipped an hour ago, and rollback means finding the right prior code commit instead of reassigning an alias. Overhead (a registration call + alias reassignment) is small relative to the cost of an unreviewed regression reaching users. Would change the recommendation given a track record showing this system's prompt changes never caused a measurable regression across a meaningful sample -- and even then, keep at minimum a lightweight versioned history rather than fully unversioned strings.

drills.q: Explain the distinction between 'the pipeline didn't change' and 'the data didn't change,' with a concrete failure example.
drills.a: A training pipeline reading a live source table can run identical code against silently mutated underlying data (a backfill, a schema migration, new rows landing) between two runs -- the pipeline is unchanged but the data isn't, and without an explicit immutable data version tagged per run, this produces an unreproducible model even though 'nothing changed' from the code's perspective.
